title: Brightness and Voltage
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Brightness and Voltage Worksheets (Cells, Lamps and Buzzers)
standard_text: Associate the brightness of a lamp or the volume of a buzzer with the number and voltage of cells used in the circuit.
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on brightness and voltage: how the number and voltage of cells changes lamp brightness, buzzer volume and motor speed, with circuit comparisons and investigations. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Voltage pushes current; extra lamps in series share it and get dimmer.
body_html:
How to think about it

More voltage makes components work harder; more components share the voltage.

  • Each cell is usually 1.5 V. Cells in a line add up: 3 cells = 4.5 V.
  • More cells: brighter lamps, louder buzzers, faster motors.
  • More lamps in series share the voltage, so each one is dimmer. Too many cells can blow a lamp.
Example

4 cells of 1.5 V. Total?

4 × 1.5

Answer: 6 V

Example

2 cells, 1 lamp vs 2 cells, 2 lamps. Brighter?

One lamp gets all the voltage

Answer: the single lamp

Common mistakes

  • Thinking adding a lamp makes both lamps brighter.
  • Thinking two 1.5 V cells give 1.5 V.
  • Thinking any number of cells is safe for a lamp.

faq.q: Why does adding cells make a lamp brighter?
faq.a: Each cell adds voltage, which pushes more current through the lamp, so it glows brighter (up to what the lamp can safely take).

faq.q: Why are two lamps dimmer than one?
faq.a: In a series circuit the two lamps share the same voltage from the cells, so each gets less and glows less brightly.

faq.q: How do you work out the voltage of a battery?
faq.a: Add the voltages of the cells joined in a line. Three 1.5 V cells make 4.5 V.
